report: Conclusion: the claim is **unsupported/misleading**. Capsaicin has shown anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects against breast-cancer cells in culture and in mouse xenograft models, but that is preclinical evidence, not proof that it treats human breast cancer (https://www.nature.com/articles/onc2009335). Reviews of the broader capsaicin–cancer literature describe abundant laboratory and animal work yet emphasize that oral capsaicin’s clinical value as a chemotherapy complement remains speculative; human use is mainly topical for pain/neuropathy, not tumor eradication (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2022.908487/full). I found no retrieved evidence of completed human trials showing capsaicin shrinks breast tumors or improves survival. Established breast-cancer care remains surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, endocrine and targeted therapies selected by stage and biology (https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/hp/breast-treatment-pdq). Practical advice: do not substitute capsaicin or chili supplements for oncology care; discuss any complementary use with the treating team because dose, GI/skin toxicity, drug interactions and product quality are concerns. Eating moderate spicy food appears generally safe, but “treats breast cancer in humans” is not currently true.
